# Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 11 (Bi-Vb Pc11)

**ID:** Bi-Vb Pc11  
**Section:** Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga (bi-vb)  
**Collection:** Vinaya  
**Title (Pali):** Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 11  
**Title (English, from literature):** Meeting a man in the dark  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/vin02m1.mul7.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/vin02m1.mul7.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 11, entitled *Rattandhakāra* ("Meeting a man in the dark"), governs situations where a Buddhist nun remains alone in darkness with a male interlocutor [Hüsken 1997]. The rule establishes that if a nun, one-on-one, stands together with or converses with a man in the darkness of night where there is no light (*yā pana bhikkhunī rattandhakāre appadīpe purisena saddhiṁ eken’ ekā santiṭṭheyya vā sallapeyya vā*), she incurs an offense requiring confession (*pācittiya*) [Hüsken 1997]. In the background origin story, a nun is depicted standing and speaking with a male relative [Hüsken 1997]. Commenting on this formulation, the *Samantapāsādikā* glosses "without light" (*appadīpe*) as a place unilluminated by any lamp, moon, sun, or fire [Hüsken 1997].

While there is no identical rule in the Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga, Pācittiya 11 forms the beginning of a cohesive sequence of four Bhikkhunī rules (Pācittiyas 11–14) that forbid nuns from standing together with or conversing with a man in specific secluded or compromising circumstances, such as in the dark, in hidden places, or on public streets and crossroads [Hüsken 1997]. An English translation of the text is provided by Bhikkhu Brahmali.

Curated parallels to the rule exist across the Vinaya traditions of multiple early schools, including the Pali Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha and Parivāra, the Chinese recensions of the Dharmaguptaka (*Pc 86*), Mahīśāsaka (*Pc 128*), Sarvāstivāda (*Pc 84*), and Mahāsāṅghika (*Pc 123*), as well as the Sanskrit Mahāsāṅghika-Lokottaravādin Bhikṣuṇī Vibhaṅga (*san-lo-bi-vb-pc123*).
